news.title: Lawsuit says Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made illegal agreement on AI slowdown
news.text:
A new lawsuit claims Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made an illegal deal to slow the pace of their respective AI development.

The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, argues that the leading AI companies violated antitrust laws when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts, and that doing so would reduce the value consumers get for paid AI subscriptions.

The coordination largely took place on Sept. 12, the lawsuit argues, when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging for industrywide cooperation on decelerating advancements in favor of enhanced safety measures. That same day, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk and Google DeepMind's co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis each publicly responded to Amodei's proposals in agreement.

But the lawsuit also alleges that the coordination began to take shape months earlier. It points to a statement from July 2026 that high-ranking employees from several of the leading AI labs signed that acknowledged the "intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow" development. That statement called on the government to support a global effort to slow automated AI development.

It is clear that an agreement among the chief rivals in AI that their progress "should be slower than competition would otherwise produce has an anticompetitive effect on consumers," the plaintiffs argue.

Lawyers representing four named plaintiffs, who pay for subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok or Gemini, are bringing the lawsuit on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of other paid subscribers to those services.

The plaintiffs don't object to the companies individually deciding to slow their own progress in favor of safety. They instead argue in the complaint that antitrust laws forbid them from taking the "shortcut" of agreeing to "substitute collective restraint for individual accountability." A competitive market allows for responsibility and genuine progress, the lawsuit argues.

"AI will quickly spin out of human control and could kill us all if we allow AI safety and protocol ... to be controlled by private self-serving agreements between the world's most powerful 'for profit' technology companies," said Nick Rowley, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs.

Representatives for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceXAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

In his initial essay proposing the slowdown, Amodei acknowledged potential antitrust challenges, writing that it would be helpful for the U.S. government to mediate "or at least enable" these cross-lab discussions. The government wouldn't need to participate, he wrote, but it would need to "issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations."

In response, Altman said on social media that OpenAI welcomes the idea of a "federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements," but said "we do not believe we need to wait for an antitrust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence."

While the recent conversations about pacing development were spurred by increasing concerns about AI evading human control, several leaders in the AI space have long talked about developing a shared set of standards or otherwise coordinating to ensure safety efforts remain paramount.

The plaintiffs in the lawsuit contend they are not against the AI companies asking Congress, the White House or any other agency to develop AI regulation, nor are they against the companies asking for an antitrust exemption.

But achieving that kind of collaboration with the federal government could be an uphill battle.

President Donald Trump rejected the calls for regulation on social media. He has claimed that any efforts to limit the technology are part of a "conspiracy." He called into question why the industry leaders would be calling for regulation that, he says, "if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy." Trump said Saturday on social media that he is forming an AI task force and will appoint an "AI czar," but he provided scant detail.

The Trump administration has been vocal about wanting American AI labs to outpace and excel against Chinese competition. While several Democratic leaders and candidates have called for sweeping action on AI regulation, Republicans have largely mirrored Trump's position.

Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, said in a recent Senate hearing that "there is no world" in which he would agree to give "the most powerful companies in the history of the world" an exemption from antitrust laws to collaborate, arguing that they could collude together and stifle competition.
news.summary: The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, argues that the leading AI companies violated antitrust laws when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts, and that doing so would reduce the value consumers get for paid AI subscriptions.

news.title: Trump escalates media battle by barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House claiming 'fake news'
news.text: The uproar in the United States continued Saturday evening over President Donald Trump’s extraordinary decision to bar reporters from CNN, MS NOW — formerly MSNBC — and Politico from entering the White House, saying he had had enough of the “fake news” they allegedly spread about him. Journalists from all three outlets said that when they tried to enter the complex Saturday, their credentials were confiscated, while CNN and MS NOW correspondents were forced to broadcast from a sidewalk on a nearby street. Trump’s ban marks the latest escalation in his long-running battle with a range of U.S. media organizations since returning to the White House last year. Although he also attacked the mainstream media throughout his first term — and helped turn the phrase “fake news” into a fixture of political discourse — he generally stopped short of measures this sweeping. During his second term, however, he has intensified his campaign against various news organizations. He has filed multiple lawsuits against newspapers and television networks over reports he objected to, including a $10 billion suit against The Wall Street Journal over its report that he once sent a birthday greeting featuring a drawing of a naked woman to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. He has repeatedly urged the Federal Communications Commission to punish networks over content he disliked, sought to have Jimmy Kimmel’s late-night show canceled and frequently insulted journalists — particularly female reporters — when they asked him difficult questions. Trump had already imposed a partial boycott on a major news organization last year, barring Associated Press reporters from joining the regular press pool that accompanies him in the Oval Office, aboard Air Force One and at other events. The move came in retaliation for the AP’s decision not to adopt his preferred name, “Gulf of America,” for the Gulf of Mexico. The AP challenged the restriction in court, in a case that remains ongoing, but until now Trump had stopped short of completely banning the agency from the White House — the step he has now taken against CNN, MS NOW and Politico. It remains unclear why he singled out those three outlets while continuing to label many others “fake news,” including The New York Times and The Washington Post, which were not included in the ban. “I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, Fake News CNN, MS NOW, and Politico are banned from the White House as a result of their constant false reporting,” Trump wrote Friday. He added that “media outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” At an Oval Office event Friday, Trump added: “I don’t think somebody should be allowed to come in and write false stories, fake news, and that’s why they have no credibility. During the election, 96% of my coverage was negative, and yet I won, because they have no credibility. If they want to write it, let them write it — but I don’t have to let them into the White House. It’s sick.” Politico reported that the move caught many senior White House officials by surprise and noted that Trump announced it while his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, was away from Washington. It was not initially clear Friday night whether the ban had actually taken effect. But when journalists from the three outlets tried to enter the White House Saturday morning, they were told their credentials were no longer valid and the passes were taken from them. MS NOW correspondent Akayla Gardner said that at one entrance, a security officer asked her to hand over her badge. “He said it had been disabled. I asked why I couldn’t go inside, and he said it was above him,” she said while broadcasting from a sidewalk nearby. CNN senior White House reporter Betsy Klein described a similar experience. She said that when she asked for her badge back, the security officer returned only the plastic sleeve it had originally come in. She vowed to keep reporting on the White House. “We’re going to keep doing our jobs, whether that’s inside the White House complex or right here at the intersection nearby. We can do our jobs anywhere,” she said. The three media organizations signaled that they intend to take legal action against the ban, arguing that it violates the First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and freedom of the press. “We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Politico’s global editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger said. CNN called the ban an “illegal assault” on press freedom and said the network “will not be deterred from its mission to scrutinize the administration and other public institutions and hold them accountable.” MS NOW said it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.” A range of U.S. journalists and news organizations also issued statements expressing solidarity with the barred outlets. Among the most notable came from Jacqui Heinrich, a correspondent for conservative Fox News — Trump’s favored network — who also serves as president of the White House Correspondents’ Association. “The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” she said. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask.” “This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.” Heinrich said the White House Correspondents’ Association “stands in defense of our colleagues” at the three organizations, who she said were being singled out “for doing their jobs.” Amy Kristin Sanders, a Penn State University professor and expert in media law, told the Associated Press that the Trump administration “is not interested in operating under the traditional First Amendment rules and norms.” She warned that the president’s actions could have consequences for press freedom beyond the United States. “The Trump administration’s efforts to undermine press freedom and challenge the legitimacy of independent journalism go far beyond those of any other modern American president,” she said. “It would not be an exaggeration to say that his hostile actions toward media organizations and individual journalists are chilling free expression around the world.” CNN media correspondent Brian Stelter also called the move “a direct threat to press freedom in the United States.” “This is much bigger than CNN,” he said. “This is a test of free speech in America.”
news.summary: Reporters from the three outlets had credentials confiscated and were forced to broadcast from outside the White House, as the organizations threatened legal action and press groups warned of a broader threat to First Amendment rights

news.title: On trophies from Paris and farewells to Jacobs and Peter
news.text:
By the time you’re reading this, President Bola Tinubu is probably concluding his 21-day holiday in Europe, where he’s been mode-switching from rest, work and scheming ahead of the January elections.

The past three weeks have been one of those times when the forecourt of the Aso Rock Villa falls quiet, and the parking lots stay empty until the big man returns.

Last Sunday, the President arrived in Paris for the second leg of his European holiday. For those who observed, the president swapped the order of his holiday destinations this year. Last September, he began his holiday in Paris and planned to conclude in London, until he abruptly changed his mind and flew to Kaduna for the wedding of the son of former Zamfara State Governor, Senator Abdul’aziz Yari.

Politics and conjugal celebrations are two sides of the same coin. Incidentally, however, U.S. President Donald Trump was scheduled to begin his state visit to the UK that week.

In my earlier pieces, I explored what I argued was the hide-and-seek relationship between the two men. My observations will be further proven if Tinubu defies all earlier arrangements and does not show up at this year’s United Nations General Assembly in New York. I’ll leave it at that.

So the past week saw the president engage in various forms of remote work. From Paris, he moved the digital free zones from paperwork to implementation, targeting global jobs for young Nigerians who currently export themselves because their skills cannot find a local buyer.

From Paris, too, came Tinubu’s arguably sweetest news for the week, when, on Thursday, an International Chamber of Commerce tribunal sitting in that same city threw out the claims by Sunrise Power and Transmission Company against Nigeria, and ordered the firm and its promoter, Mr Leno Adesanya, to refund most of the Federal Government’s $11.82m legal bill.

Sunrise had demanded $680m in settlement and interest, tied to a separate claim of more than $2.7bn over the 3,960MW Mambilla Hydroelectric Power Project. The President called it “the single biggest legal hurdle” that had paralysed Mambilla for over two decades, a project born out of a 2003 contract the Federal Executive Council reportedly never authorised.

Then came the roll call of gratitude, where Tinubu commended the Attorney General, Lateef Fagbemi, the Paul Hastings defence team led by Elizabeth Oger-Gross and Tolu Obamuroh, the NSA, the EFCC, and then former President Olusegun Obasanjo and the late President Muhammadu Buhari, both of whom testified for Nigeria in the Paris arbitration.

And from Paris, the President is reportedly trying to broker peace between the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, and aggrieved APC governors. Such a quarrel, if left to fester, could curdle into something ugly for the governing party’s campaign. 

However, the weeks also came with their own gloom. The first was the loss of the Assistant Director of Information and Public Relations at the Presidential Villa, Peter Onwubuariri, who died in Kano at 48 after a prolonged illness and was buried in Owerri.

The President called his passing “a painful loss to the Presidency, the News Agency of Nigeria, the media community and the nation.” Presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga led the media team to Peter’s home in Abuja.

Mr Tunde Rahman called the late official a workaholic who never returned an assignment unless it was excellent.

They are a thousand times right, all of them. From my perspective, however, Peter was more than an official. Being the avid reader that he was, he always had some insightful feedback on my writings that kept me looking forward to seeing him.

It was Peter who once told me, almost in passing, that I was the reporter filing the most exclusives on President Tinubu’s much-anticipated ambassadorial appointments from late 2023 right through to the eventual postings in late 2025.

He had been counting. I had not. That is the kind of man Peter was. He was watchful enough to notice the good work of others and generous enough to tell you when you were winning.

He read my copy and offered feedback drawn from years of serving on the media teams of three presidents: Jonathan, Buhari and Tinubu. In an environment where information is currency, and most people guard their tokens, Peter gave freely, out of the abundance of his experience and his desire to see me do better. “Punch Man! Punch Man!! Which exclusive are you looking for today?” he would say when we met in the corridors. Go well, Peter. Rest well, Uncle Peter.

On Thursday, the country lost another institution, veteran actor Olu Jacobs, who died at 84. The President called him “a giant of the Nigerian creative industry,” whose body of work “will continue to speak to generations yet unborn.”

For me, he will always be Chief Udensi in the 1998 home video Obstacles. His unmistakable voice, his carriage of authority and, much later, the gems of wisdom on the various forums he has spoken on are what I will remember him for. Our condolences to his family.
news.summary:
President Bola Tinubu’s trip to Paris sees a major legal victory for Nigeria over the Mambilla project, alongside tributes to the late Olu Jacobs and Peter

news.title: Trump says he will form new 'AI Force' but continues to call AI fears a 'hoax'
news.text:
As concerns from Silicon Valley and beyond grow about the rapid pace of AI development, President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would move to create a new "AI Force" and promised to appoint a new AI czar as he continued to defend the technology.

Referring to the fears around AI alignment as a "hoax," Trump asserted in a post on social media that "we will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," adding, "rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"

However, Trump said in order to look out for the "bad" aspects of AI, the U.S. would form an "AI Force," likening it to the formation of Space Force during his first term, and said he would appoint an AI czar in the "near future."

It is unclear what the "AI Force" would be tasked with doing.

Space Force -- which falls under the purview of the Department of Defense -- was created by an act of Congress as a sixth branch of the U.S. Armed Forces in 2020. Another armed forces branch would require further action from Congress.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump appeared to reject the idea that new regulations were needed to protect the wider world from the threat of misaligned AI systems, asserting that the U.S. could already do so within the existing legal framework.

"We will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System," Trump wrote in the post announcing the new "AI Force."

Trump's announcement comes amid warnings from top tech leaders about the potential dangers of AI.

Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post calling to slow the pace of AI development. Shortly afterward, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said his company would also welcome a slower development pace to ensure that the technology's capabilities don't "get ahead of alignment and monitoring."

Some lawmakers have also called for more guardrails around AI development.

At the time Trump responded that the warnings were a "HOAX" and that there was a "SICK conspiracy" going on around AI.

The president's latest comments announcing the new "AI Force" echoed that of David Sacks, co-chair of Trump's science and technology council, who indicated at a Politico conference on Wednesday that more regulations were not necessarily needed.

"I think the starting point for talking about AI regulation is to realize the regulations that we already have," said Sacks, who previously served as the White House's former AI and crypto czar until stepping down in March.

"We have a highly regulated administrative state, and we already have a lot of laws and regulations that pertain to AI. And we have a lot of administrative agencies that promulgate regulations related to AI," Sacks said.
news.summary: Trump likened the new entity to Space Force and also said he would name an AI czar.
news.author: Houston,Nicholas Kerr

news.title: Gavin Newsom Signs California Tax Credit to Retain Hollywood Jobs
news.text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom is unveiling another multimillion-dollar boost for Hollywood, this time focused on keeping film and television editors, visual effects professionals and other behind-the-scenes talent working in California.

Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2319 on Friday at the Television Academy in North Hollywood. The law creates what supporters call the nation’s first California tax credit dedicated specifically to post-production.

The new incentive will cover 35% to 50% of eligible post-production spending in California, including editing, sound, music, visual effects and final finishing work.

The program also breaks from California’s existing film and television incentive by allowing projects to qualify even if they are not filmed in the state.

Under the current program, post-production expenses qualify when at least 75% of a project’s filming or total production budget is spent in California. The new credit instead aims to bring post-production jobs to the state while allowing principal photography to take place elsewhere.

“This is a big victory in our fight to save California’s entertainment industry, and we’re just getting started,” said Assemblyman Nick Schultz, a Burbank Democrat who introduced the bill.

“This program will literally save jobs here in Los Angeles and across the state,” Schultz said. “When California competes, we all win.”

Even so, the initiative begins at a far smaller scale than its backers had hoped.

Schultz originally proposed allocating $100 million to the post-production credit, a figure supported by the Motion Picture Editors Guild. Lawmakers ultimately approved $10 million—just 10% of the initial request.

The new incentive arrives as California faces growing pressure from states and countries offering competing tax breaks to attract post-production work.

CVL Economics data cited by the Los Angeles Times shows California’s share of U.S. post-production employment falling from 53% to 42% over the last 13 years. The consulting firm, which is affiliated with the California Post Alliance, estimated that the state had roughly 12,000 post-production jobs last year.

That decline has been especially painful for workers navigating Hollywood’s broader employment slump.

Ben Urquhart, a 51-year-old Culver City resident, told the Times that he spent 18 years as a post-production executive at NBCUniversal before losing his job. Two and a half years after the layoff, he said he remains unemployed.

“It’s grim and it’s hard. There are jobs, but we have a large amount of extremely qualified people competing for every level of job,” Urquhart said.

He contrasted today’s market with his experience as a production assistant in the 1990s, when landing another job could take only a few weeks.

California recently expanded its Film and Television Tax Credit Program from $330 million to $750 million per year. The higher funding level is authorized through June 30, 2030.

Urquhart said the additional post-production incentive could help California catch up with jurisdictions that already offer similar credits and “level the playing field.”

The legislation is part of Sacramento’s larger push to keep Hollywood production—and the jobs tied to it—rooted in California.

“California is the nation’s entertainment capital,” Newsom said in a statement. “It is the home of storytellers, dreamers, artists, entrepreneurs, and creators who define culture for the rest of the world.”

Newsom’s office said 170 projects announced since the broader incentive expansion are projected to produce more than $6.6 billion in economic activity and nearly 35,000 cast and crew jobs across the state.

Newsom also signed Senate Bill 186, which makes changes to the existing incentive program, including enhanced refundability and relief for certain independent productions from a temporary limitation on tax credits beginning in 2027.

The push to lure entertainment jobs is also reaching Washington. President Donald Trump has publicly supported the idea of a federal film tax credit, while Reps. Laura Friedman, D-Calif., and Brian Jack, R-Ga., are leading a bipartisan effort to draft one, according to the Times.

Newsom capped off Friday’s Hollywood push with a visit to the Burbank set of HBO Max’s “The Pitt,” as California tries to keep more of Hollywood’s work in the Golden State.

news.title: Alert from health officials as it emerges person with measles traveled from Chicago to LA by train
news.text:
A traveler infected with measles may have spread the highly contagious disease while riding an Amtrak train from Chicago to Los Angeles and then taking trains and buses across at least six California counties and a train to Denver.

The unidentified person, who wasn’t vaccinated against measles, was hospitalized after the five-day trip from September 10 to 15, according to the California Department of Public Health, which on Friday urged Golden State residents to protect themselves by getting vaccinated.

“This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles,” Dr. Rita Nguyen, the state's assistant health officer, said in a statement. “Measles is one of the most contagious infections that can lead to severe life-long consequences including permanent brain damage and can also be fatal, especially for children.”

The CDPH posted the traveler's itinerary online and said anyone who was on the trains or buses, or was at the stations on the relevant days, may have been exposed to measles. 

It also noted that the traveler's scheduled arrival and departure times may differ from the actual times, and said state health officials were working with federal and county officials to notify the people who may be at risk.

The disturbing development came as the U.S. is grappling with a record measles caseload that's the highest since 1991, according to the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research & Policy.

The nation has experienced multiple measles outbreaks in 45 states and the District of Columbia this year, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reporting 3,471 confirmed cases as of Friday.

Only five states — Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire — haven't reported any infections, according to the CDC.

Ninety-five percent of the confirmed cases involve people who haven't been vaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown.

Pennsylvania has recorded four measles related deaths, but they're not listed on the CDC's website, which says that the National Center for Health Statistics “does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.”

President Donald Trump's health secretary, former environmental lawyer and vaccine critic Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has repeatedly downplayed America’s rash of measles cases by blaming them on a global epidemic and claiming the U.S. is handling it better than other countries.

Measles data compiled by the World Health Organization show that the U.S. had 13.2 measles cases per 1 million people this year, as of September 14, FactCheck.org reported Friday.

That rate makes America No. 65 for the highest rate of infection among 169 countries with measles data, or among the worst 38 percent, according to FactCheck.org.

“There are countries that are sort of peer countries — you know, peer developed countries — which have very, very little, basically no outbreaks of measles,” Josh Michaud, an associate director of global and public health policy at the health policy research organization KFF, told the website.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services didn't immediately respond to a Saturday inquiry from The Independent.
news.summary: The unidentified traveler also rode buses and trains across six California counties before taking a train to Denver

news.title: Donald Trump's Approval Ratings Loom Over Midterms With 45 Days to Go
news.text: With 45 days remaining until the midterm elections, Republicans face a question that could determine control of Congress: How much does President Donald Trump's unpopularity matter? Midterm elections are often seen as referendums on the party occupying the White House. This year, Republicans are hoping that concerns about immigration, crime and national security will outweigh voter dissatisfaction with Trump. Democrats, meanwhile, are betting that frustration over inflation, gasoline prices and the president's handling of the Iran war will translate into victories up and down the ballot. Control of both the House and Senate remains within reach for either party, raising the stakes of Trump's standing with voters as Election Day approaches. Newsweek reached out to the White House for comment on Saturday. Why Trump's Approval Matters Republicans point to Trump's 2024 victory despite years of unfavorable approval ratings. His supporters have repeatedly proven more loyal at the ballot box than many polling analysts expected. But governing and winning a midterm election are different challenges. A growing body of polling suggests Trump's ratings remain underwater nationally, even as Republicans seek to energize voters ahead of November. Nathan Gonzales, editor and publisher of Inside Elections, said Trump's standing has created a challenging political environment for Republicans. "Any midterm election with an unpopular president is potentially treacherous for his party," Gonzales told Newsweek on Saturday. At the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month, Trump urged supporters to act as though he himself were on the ballot this November, further tying Republican candidates to perceptions of his presidency. "Pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot, just one more time," Trump told the crowd. The Numbers Behind Trump's Standing A Marquette Law School survey found 37 percent of adults approved of Trump's job performance and 63 percent disapproved, the weakest result of his second term in the poll. The same polling environment has contributed to broader concerns about Republican prospects in November. The survey also found Democrats leading Republicans 54 percent to 41 percent on the congressional ballot among likely voters. Other polls have produced somewhat different numbers while reaching a similar conclusion. A recent Fox News survey found Trump's job approval rating at 39 percent, while a Reuters/Ipsos poll put it at 35 percent. Both were national surveys of voters, indicating Trump's challenges are not confined to a single battleground state or region. Both surveys found a majority of voters disapproved of Trump's performance. A Referendum Republicans Didn't Expect When Republicans entered 2026, many expected the election to focus on border security, immigration and public safety, issues where the party historically performs well. Instead, much of the national conversation has centered on pocketbook concerns. Polls have consistently shown inflation and the cost of living among voters' top concerns. The Marquette Law School survey found inflation and the cost of living were the country's top concerns, cited by 37 percent of respondents. Many Americans continue to report paying more for groceries and gasoline than they did earlier in the year, creating a difficult political environment for an administration struggling to convince voters that economic conditions are improving. The Iran war has also emerged as a political complication. A recent Fox News poll found a majority of voters believe U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, while nearly three-quarters said the administration lacks a clear plan for ending the conflict. Even if foreign policy ranks below economic concerns, such findings suggest voters remain skeptical about one of Trump's most consequential decisions since returning to office. The Independent Voter Problem Perhaps the greatest warning sign for Republicans isn't what core Trump supporters think. It's what appears to be happening with voters in the middle. An August I&I/TIPP national survey found Trump's approval rating among independents fell from 29 percent to 26 percent while disapproval rose from 59 percent to 61 percent, highlighting concerns about a voting bloc that often helps decide close races. The consequences are already visible. Gonzales said Democrats do not necessarily need a wave election to make major gains. Instead, he argued that Republican weaknesses have opened opportunities in places that were not expected to be competitive earlier in the cycle. Gonzales added that "the president's poor job approval rating has laid the foundation for Democrats to win in states where they normally don't have any business competing.” North Carolina, one of the most important Senate battlegrounds in the country, has produced a string of surveys showing Democrat Roy Cooper ahead of Republican Michael Whatley. In Texas, Republicans are suddenly being forced to spend time defending races they likely expected would be less competitive. Republicans Still Have a Path None of this means Democrats are destined to win. Republicans continue to hold advantages in many individual races. The party remains competitive on immigration and border security, issues that remain important to large segments of the electorate. Trump also retains a loyal political base capable of reshaping turnout dynamics in ways conventional polling sometimes struggles to capture. Political scientists caution that disapproval of a president does not necessarily translate into votes for the opposing party. "Voting for a Democratic alternative is a higher bar than stating lack of approval," Grant Reeher, a political science professor at Syracuse University, recently told Newsweek. "But it suggests more about potential turnout effects than vote choice. And in a midterm, that's really important." Republicans argue that Trump's political strengths will outweigh concerns about his approval ratings. "President Trump cut taxes, lowered prescription drug costs, and secured our border, and he energizes Republican voters like no one else," Natalie Baldassarre, the Republican National Committee's national press secretary, told Newsweek on Saturday. Baldassarre said Republican candidates would campaign on what she described as Trump's achievements while drawing contrasts with Democratic policies. The White House has also argued that polling does not reflect the full impact of Trump's agenda. In a previous statement to Newsweek, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said: "No other president in history has accomplished more for the American people than President Trump, who is working tirelessly to create jobs, cool inflation, increase housing affordability, and more." Ingle added that Trump's agenda was still taking effect and that the administration had already made "historic progress" both domestically and internationally. Republicans also point to the party's advantages on immigration and border security, as well as Trump's ability to energize core supporters, as reasons they remain confident about November. Presidential approval ratings can shape the political environment, but they do not determine election outcomes on their own. Candidate quality, turnout, fundraising and local issues will also play important roles in many of the races that decide control of Congress. What to Watch in the Final 45 Days The most important indicator may not be whether Trump's approval rating rises or falls by a few points. Instead, Republicans will be watching for signs that dissatisfied supporters remain motivated enough to vote. A president can be unpopular and still help his party if supporters show up. But if concerns about the economy, inflation and foreign policy cause some Republicans to stay home, even marginal changes in turnout could have significant consequences in closely contested races. Democrats, for their part, are hoping the election becomes exactly what midterms often become: a judgment on the party in power. With 45 days remaining, the central question is no longer whether Trump will dominate the political conversation. He already does. The question is whether voters will reward him for it.
news.summary: Trump's approval numbers remain weak as Republicans race to hold Congress with 45 days until Election Day.
